checklists.name: Color System
checklists.description: The color layer of a design system — defining a palette that is purposeful, accessible, themeable, and expressed as tokens rather than raw values.

criteria.title: Primitive palette
criteria.description: A base set of named color ramps (blue-100 through blue-900, neutral-0 through neutral-1000) that serves as the raw material for all semantic decisions
criteria.suggestion: Systems where components reference primitive values directly are significantly harder to theme — a color change requires updating each component individually rather than a single token definition

criteria.title: Semantic color tokens
criteria.description: Named tokens that describe purpose rather than appearance so the system can be reskinned without touching components e.g. color-background-primary, color-text-danger, color-border-interactive
criteria.suggestion: The semantic layer is what makes a design system actually themeable by defining purpose for colors

criteria.title: Interactive state colors
criteria.description: Defined color values for default, hover, pressed, focused, disabled, and selected states applied consistently across all interactive elements

criteria.title: Feedback colors
criteria.description: A consistent set of colors for success, warning, error, and informational states — used across alerts, form validation, badges, and status indicators.
criteria.suggestion: Feedback colors that pass contrast in light mode frequently fail in dark mode — testing each token pair against every surface in both themes is where most gaps tend to surface.

criteria.title: Contrast ratios (accessibility)
criteria.description: A breakdown of text and interactive element color combinations verified to meet WCAG AA contrast minimums — 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI components
criteria.suggestion: Not all colors will pair together nicely so defining this for all usage is helpful

criteria.title: Dark and light mode definition
criteria.description: A complete parallel set of semantic token values for the opposite mode
criteria.suggestion: It is not as simple as inverting colors of one mode to the other, they require their own system (still using the same primitive colors though)

criteria.title: Brand color integration
criteria.description: Brand colors mapped into the semantic system in a way that maintains accessibility
criteria.suggestion: Where brand values fall below contrast thresholds, they are restricted to decorative contexts, with accessible token values carrying the text and interactive roles.

criteria.title: Color blindness considerations
criteria.description: The palette tested against common color vision deficiencies for when color is used to convey state
criteria.suggestion: It's worthwhile considering relative items to the color if vision is a concern, meaning an icon or text can help further convey a state incase the color is not successfully visible

criteria.title: Calendar grid
criteria.description: A month view with days arranged in a weekly grid, navigable forward and backward by month, as the primary date selection surface

criteria.title: Text input alongside
criteria.description: A free-text date field paired with the calendar, so users who know the date can type it rather than relying on clicking only
criteria.suggestion: Suitable for when you know dates selected may be months or years away e.g. date of birth

criteria.title: Date range selection (if applicable)
criteria.description: The ability to select a start and end date, with the range highlighted across the calendar grid and both values independently editable

criteria.title: Disabled dates
criteria.description: Past dates, unavailable dates, or out-of-range dates visually distinct from selectable ones

criteria.title: Today shortcut
criteria.description: A clearly labelled button or link to jump to today's date

criteria.title: Locale and format
criteria.description: The calendar respecting regional conventions e.g. week starting on Monday or Sunday, date format in the text input matching the user's locale (DD/MM or MM/DD)

criteria.title: Time selection (if applicable)
criteria.description: When a time is also required, a time picker integrated with or accessible directly from the date picker (not a separate, disconnected control)

checklists.name: Drawer
checklists.description: A drawer is a panel that slides in from the edge, overlaying content. It provides access to detailed information without completely navigating away from the current page.

criteria.title: Placement
criteria.description: Which edge the drawer slides from - most commonly from left (navigation) or right (details/settings)

criteria.title: Dimensions
criteria.description: Typically full height, but width can vary. Should be wide enough for complex content to be shown, without taking over the entire page

criteria.title: Overlay
criteria.description: A semi-transparent background for the remaining screen area to bring focus to the drawer

criteria.title: Header
criteria.description: Top section with a title describing drawer contents or purpose, along with a close action (optional)
criteria.suggestion: Can also include a description of drawer contents if header is too simple

criteria.title: Content area
criteria.description: Main section, which should be scrollable if content exceeds window height

criteria.title: Open and close trigger
criteria.description: How user activate the drawer — typically a button to open, while closing can have multiple ways: clicking overlay, a close button, or pressing Esc on keyboard should all be active options

criteria.title: Footer
criteria.description: Fixed area at the bottom for actions, usually a primary and secondary e.g. Save & Cancel

resources.title: Placement
resources.description: Best practices are left for navigation, right for anything else

resources.title: Overlay
resources.description: Ensure it brings enough focus to the drawer (considering using same overlay as modal)

resources.title: Content layout
resources.description: The anatomy of a drawer

checklists.name: Spacing / Grid
checklists.description: The spatial layer of a design system, defining a consistent scale for spacing, a grid for layout, and the rules that make both feel deliberate and coherent across all surfaces.

criteria.title: Spacing scale
criteria.description: A defined set of spacing values (typically base-4 or base-8, covering 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96) used for all margin, padding, and gap decisions
criteria.suggestion: A base-8 scale is the most commonly adopted because it divides evenly across common device pixel ratios and helps avoid exceptions being made

criteria.title: Semantic spacing tokens
criteria.description: Named tokens for spacing that describe purpose (space-component-padding-sm, space-layout-section-gap) so spacing decisions are intentional, not arbitrary
criteria.suggestion: Raw spacing values appearing as hardcoded numbers in components make global spacing changes significantly harder, since each instance requires a separate update rather than a single token edit

criteria.title: Column grid
criteria.description: A defined column grid for each major breakpoint (typically 4 columns mobile, 8 tablet, 12 desktop) with gutter and margin values specified

criteria.title: Breakpoints
criteria.description: A named set of breakpoints (sm, md, lg, xl) that are shared between design and code, so responsive behaviour is described in consistent terms across both disciplines
criteria.suggestion: Breakpoint names tied to device types (phone, tablet, desktop) tend to age poorly as screen sizes shift. Content-based naming (narrow, mid, wide) describes viewport behaviour rather than hardware categories

criteria.title: Component vs layout spacing
criteria.description: A clear distinction between spacing used inside components and spacing used to compose layouts, since different scales often apply to each
criteria.suggestion: Buttons that use the same spacing tokens as page-level section gaps, and vice versa, tend to produce compositions where internal padding and layout rhythm feel mismatched

criteria.title: Density variants
criteria.description: Where applicable, defined compact and comfortable density modes, common in data-heavy products where users need to choose between information density and breathing room

criteria.title: Baseline grid alignment
criteria.description: Text baselines and component heights designed to align to the base unit, so stacking elements produces predictable, harmonious vertical rhythm

checklists.name: Tokens
checklists.description: The layer of a design system where defined variables are outlined across the platform to enable consistency, theming and alignment with code.

criteria.title: Three-tier token architecture
criteria.description: Tokens organised into primitive, semantic, and component tiers — primitives store raw values, semantic tokens describe purpose, component tokens scope decisions to a specific element
criteria.suggestion: It's okay to start with just primitives and component tokens first, and only utilise semantic for theming

criteria.title: Naming convention
criteria.description: A consistent, predictable naming pattern so any token name communicates its purpose without needing documentation.
criteria.suggestion: A token named blue-500 tells you the value, but a token named color-interactive-primary-default tells you when and where to use it, making that system the scalable one

criteria.title: Token documentation
criteria.description: Each semantic token documented with its intended use, example contexts, and what it can and cannot be used for

criteria.title: Token governance
criteria.description: A clear rule for what constitutes a token versus a hardcoded value, and a process for reviewing and approving new tokens before they are added to the system
criteria.suggestion: New tokens should always be suggested, but have clear reasoning of purpose and scalable use to be genuinely considered

criteria.title: Design tool sync
criteria.description: Tokens maintained in your design tool of choice as variables
criteria.suggestion: Aim to find a way to connect your tokens to what is in code — naming convention being 1:1 is ideal for ongoing maintenance

criteria.title: Versioning and changelog
criteria.description: Token changes versioned and communicated in a way that teams consuming the token system can know when values change and what the impact will be on their surfaces

checklists.name: Typography
checklists.description: The type layer of a design system that defines a scale, hierarchy, and set of text styles that is consistent, accessible, and expressive across the full range of product contexts

criteria.title: Type scale
criteria.description: A defined set of font sizes with a consistent ratio between them, covering everything from captions to display headings
criteria.suggestion: A modular scale (1.25, 1.333, 1.5 ratio) produces a more harmonious hierarchy than arbitrary size choices

criteria.title: Semantic text styles
criteria.description: Named styles that describe role rather than size so usage is driven by meaning, not pixel values e.g. display-large, body-default, label-small, caption
criteria.suggestion: Style names chosen by size — 24px, 18px, 14px — consistently result in designers selecting styles by measurement rather than role, which makes the system harder to evolve when the scale changes.

criteria.title: Typeface selection and loading
criteria.description: The chosen typefaces detailing style and weight e.g. Inclusive Sans Medium

criteria.title: Line height per style
criteria.description: Line height defined explicitly for every text style since tightly spaced headings and readable body text require different values
criteria.suggestion: Similar style groups follow a consistent line height e.g. 1.5 for body text, 1.2 for heading and 1.1 for display

criteria.title: Letter spacing per style
criteria.description: Letter spacing defined per style where needed
criteria.suggestion: Similar to line height, where style groups often following a consistent pattern

criteria.title: Responsive type behaviour
criteria.description: How text styles respond to viewport size, whether through fluid type scaling, breakpoint-based overrides, or fixed sizes with responsive layout compensation

criteria.title: Minimum readable size
criteria.description: The smallest text size in use across the system, and how readability at that size is validated in the actual rendering environment
criteria.suggestion: Consider minimum size between desktop and mobile differently

criteria.title: Accessibility responsiveness
criteria.description: How text styles behave at 200% browser zoom, and whether any style communicates meaning through colour variation alone

checklists.name: Accordion
checklists.description: An accordion is a vertically stacked list of items that reveal or hide associated content sections when clicked. They help organize information hierarchically and saves screen space by showing only relevant content.

criteria.title: Header
criteria.description: The clickable area that triggers expanding and collapsing and has a title
criteria.suggestion: The header text should clearly convey the content that is inside

criteria.title: Expand/collapse icon
criteria.description: Visual indicator of the current state — typically a plus/minus, or a caret/chevron that rotates between states

criteria.title: Content area
criteria.description: The content that shows or hides when toggled, containing detailed information associated with the header
criteria.suggestion: While headers should be text only, content can be anything that is suited to help answer or elaborate on the header (text, image, video, etc)

criteria.title: States
criteria.description: Default (collapsed), expanded, hover, focused, and disabled

criteria.title: Expanding logic
criteria.description: Decide if users can open multiple sections at once, or one at a time
criteria.suggestion: Can be determined by whether you think information from other items are related and should be seen together

resources.title: Choice of icon
resources.description: Can be a plus (expanded) or minus (collapsed), or a caret/chevron that rotates on trigger

resources.title: States
resources.description: Default (collapsed), expanded, hover, and disabled

resources.title: Style
resources.description: Accordion style can change based on overall design system style (container, lines, cards)

checklists.name: Skeleton
checklists.description: A skeleton is a placeholder that mimics the structure of content while it loads. It provides visual feedback that content is coming and reduces perceived wait time.

criteria.title: Match content structure
criteria.description: Skeletons should mirror the size and layout of the content that will replace it, to reduce jumpiness on load.

criteria.title: Animation
criteria.description: Subtle motion to indicate loading without being too distracting. Can be a shimmer, pulse, or wave motion in the objects

criteria.title: Style
criteria.description: Flat shapes with no depth, can be rounded or sharp

criteria.title: Color scheme
criteria.description: Typically a neutral gray or very soft colour that does not call too much attention and contrasts just enough with its background.

criteria.title: Transition to real content
criteria.description: Should be a smooth, subtle movement like a fade out before the content loads.

resources.title: Match content structure
resources.description: Skeletons should mirror the size and layout of the content that will replace it, to reduce jumpiness on load.

resources.title: Shape variety
resources.description: Skeleton shapes can vary in width, height, radius and shape type to help differentiate content and reflect it better

checklists.name: Carousel
checklists.description: A carousel is a slideshow component that displays content one slide at a time. Users can alternate content through manual navigation or waiting for automatic transition.

criteria.title: Ways of interaction
criteria.description: Defining whether the carousel transitions are auto-play, navigated by controls, or both

criteria.title: Visual progress indicator
criteria.description: Show dots, numbers, or a progress bar so users know how many slides there are and which one they're currently viewing.
criteria.suggestion: Make the current slide's indicator look noticeably different so people can track their position at a glance.

criteria.title: Dimensions and alignment
criteria.description: The size of the items in the carousel, and their responsiveness across devices.
criteria.suggestion: Decide how content sits inside the item container so that it is filling the required space without being stretched or not looking uniform.

criteria.title: Animation behaviour
criteria.description: The direction, speed and feeling of how the items transition between each other.

criteria.title: Focused item state
criteria.description: if your carousel shows one item a time, the one on focus should appear different to the items that are entering and exiting
criteria.suggestion: Size, transparency and colour are typical properties to change on the non-focused items to allow the focused have more attention naturally

resources.title: Ways of interaction
resources.description: Defining whether the carousel transitions are auto-play, navigated by controls, or both. Auto-play: user can’t change item themselves and it is set to a routine timer. Navigated by controls = user can interact and progress to next item through action (click, drag or swipe).

resources.title: Visual progress indicator
resources.description: Show dots, numbers, or a progress bar so users know how many slides there are and which one they're currently viewing.

resources.title: Animation behaviour
resources.description: The direction, speed and feeling of how the items transition between each other.

resources.title: Focused item state
resources.description: If your carousel shows one item a time, the one on focus should appear different to the items that are entering and exiting.

checklists.name: Banner
checklists.description: A banner is a prominent notification item that displays important messages to users. It communicates things like errors, success confirmations, warnings, or general information using distinct colors and placement to stand out from regular page content and grab attention.

criteria.title: Style
criteria.description: How the banner types look (fill, text colour, border radius etc)
criteria.suggestion: Ensure the banner stands out enough on your default UI as it’s usage typically means it should not be missed

criteria.title: Content
criteria.description: A title is a must but you can consider a description if you feel a title does not convey enough information

criteria.title: Types
criteria.description: Banners typically appear as 5 options: information, success, warning, error, neutral. This helps visually establish context and level of importance.

criteria.title: Call to action button
criteria.description: A banner may call for the user to do something, like fix the error it is calling out, or viewing the successful outcome of an event.
criteria.suggestion: Only have a button if it feels needed, banners typically work best to inform

criteria.title: Placement
criteria.description: Where the banner sits on the page, dependent on context and importance
criteria.suggestion: Consider the impact the banner contents has on the user experience to determine where it’s placed best e.g. information affecting the entire application should have a banner at the top on every page. Information only affecting a small feature may be within a relevant section.

criteria.title: Dismissable
criteria.description: Whether the banner can be dismissed. Positive/neutral banners (info and success) would suit this, but not warning/error banners as they are too critical.

resources.title: Variations
resources.description: Different colours can be used to match the message type: red for errors, green for success, yellow for warnings, and blue or neutral for general information. This helps the first impression be more specific.

resources.title: Content
resources.description: It’s perfectly fine to just have 1 line of text to explain the scenario. If more details are needed, it’s good to have a short, clear title followed by a longer description. This lets people quickly scan the main message or read more if they want to.

resources.title: Actions
resources.description: An error or warning banner is common to contain an action, to take you directly to where the issue can be fixed or investigated.

resources.title: Contrast to UI
resources.description: Make banners look different from the rest of the page so they grab attention. Use background colors, borders, or shadows that make the banner clearly separate from normal page content.

resources.title: Icons
resources.description: Add simple, recognizable symbols that match the message - like checkmarks for success or warning triangles for problems. Icons help people understand the banner's meaning at a glance, even before reading the text.

resources.title: Placement
resources.description: Put banners where users will notice them relative to the context. Top of the page works for site-wide messages, while placing near related content works better for specific notifications.

checklists.name: Slider
checklists.description: A slider is an interactive control that allows users to select a value from a continuous range by dragging a handle along a track. It often provides intuitive visual feedback as it is interacted with.

criteria.title: Style
criteria.description: How the range and the handlers look visually (see documentation for inspiration)

criteria.title: Intervals
criteria.description: Whether the slider intervals has continuous (any value between 0-10000), or stepped (fixed values like a 0-5 rating)

criteria.title: Handles
criteria.description: The elements that users select to drag and change the slider value
criteria.suggestion: Handles should clearly 'break' out from the slider container to be easily identified

criteria.title: Labelling
criteria.description: Text that conveys the spectrum of the slider, or if there are intervals between those ends too

criteria.title: Interaction states
criteria.description: What the handles and slider look like when the user is changing the value

resources.title: Style
resources.description: Sliders can look different based on the context and purpose. The direction of your other design system components can influence how it should look too.

resources.title: Labels
resources.description: Labels help define the ends of your slider spectrum, or the intervals available, depending on what the slider is being used for.

resources.title: Handle interaction
resources.description: It's critical for it to be visually clear when a user is interacting with the handle to change the value.

resources.title: Tooltip
resources.description: If the slider value is more abstract, it's typical to show the value by default or on interaction, so the user understands precisely what is selected.

resources.title: Input as value
resources.description: If a slider has an extremely wide range, an input can help make it easier to define a particular value, instead of relying on the user to drag to that exact point.

checklists.name: Toast
checklists.description: A toast is a brief, non-disruptive message that appears temporarily at the edge of the screen to provide feedback about an action or system status.

criteria.title: Copy
criteria.description: The text in the toast
criteria.suggestion: Copy should be clear and concise, focusing on a status or action

criteria.title: Placement
criteria.description: Toast should appear on the corners of the viewport, not as the focus

criteria.title: Usage
criteria.description: Toasts are triggered to appear after an action or event

criteria.title: Variants
criteria.description: Dictated by colour usually, variants affects the emotion of a message
criteria.suggestion: Example: A green toast informing success, red toast informing error. If informing a status, don't rely on just color and leverage icons or the copy.

criteria.title: Length of appearance
criteria.description: Toasts should be visible long enough to read but short enough to not obstruct other information for too long
criteria.suggestion: Read the text out loud slowly to gauge how much time is needed

criteria.title: Dismissable
criteria.description: Depending on the amount of content, a toast can be closed by a user (it should fade away shortly after appearing if it cannot be manually dismissed)

resources.title: Action
resources.description: A toast can contain an action: to dismiss, or a specific action related to the context of the toast (view, undo, remove). Not every toast requires an action, so long as it disappears after a set time.

resources.title: Placement
resources.description: Toasts typically appear on the edges of an interface, to be intrusive but not interrupting. The visual represents common spots it can be placed on desktop.

resources.title: Automatic dismissal
resources.description: Toasts should stay visible enough to be acknowledged, but eventually dismiss to not intrude the interface for too long

checklists.name: Tabs
checklists.description: Tabs are navigation elements that organize and separate content into different sections within the same view. They allow users to switch between related content, maintaining context while reducing clutter.

criteria.title: Labels
criteria.description: Name of each tab
criteria.suggestion: Label should be logical enough for the user to predict what's in the tab Keep it concise, ideally 1 word

criteria.title: Content area
criteria.description: Where the content for the active tab is displayed
criteria.suggestion: Typically underneath a horizontal tab, or to the right of a vertical tab

criteria.title: Style
criteria.description: How the active tab and inactive tabs differentiate visually, as well as the tab container overall

criteria.title: Item order
criteria.description: Consider the arrangement of tabs to be ordered by popularity or familiarity

criteria.title: States
criteria.description: Default, active, hover are the key states

resources.title: Style
resources.description: How your tab container and cells look. It's important to view them in context of the UI surrounding it, to help it stay aligned

resources.title: Dynamic content
resources.description: Make sure that navigating between tabs only changes content underneath it. The user will not expect content to change above the tabs or significantly further away from the component.

resources.title: States
resources.description: These are the 3 key states, but you may also want to consider focused and disabled.

checklists.name: Checkbox
checklists.description: A checkbox is an interactive control that allows users to select or unselect items. They may be a single item to trigger other logic, or a list of multiple items to select amongst.

criteria.title: Label
criteria.description: Text paired with the checkbox to indicate what is enabled if selected

criteria.title: Default selection
criteria.description: Whether the checkbox is selected or not
criteria.suggestion: An active checkbox by default depends on its purpose - it should come down to how much this conveniences the user

criteria.title: Style
criteria.description: Make sure checkbox is unique and stands out from other input options, and consider whether it's in a container, how it's grouped, and what colour it uses

criteria.title: States
criteria.description: Default, hover, focused, active and disabled (see documentation tab for examples)

resources.title: Style
resources.description: A checkbox can be contained to make it easier to select. But if you can't afford the space for it, just the box and label are fine. It's acceptable to have both in your design system.

resources.title: States
resources.description: A breakdown of all different interactions with the checkbox

checklists.name: Radio
checklists.description: A radio button is an interactive control that allows users to select exactly one option from a predefined set of mutually exclusive choices. Unlike checkboxes, when one radio button is selected, all others in the same group are automatically deselected.

criteria.title: Label
criteria.description: Text associated with the radio input

criteria.title: Grouping
criteria.description: There must be more than one radio option for the experience to work
criteria.suggestion: Utilise radio to surface all inputs options, only being able to select one Radios with short labels can be align horizontally, but should usually be aligned vertically

criteria.title: Default selection
criteria.description: Start with a radio option selected
criteria.suggestion: This doesn't always have to be the first option, it can be the more likely option based on previous research and experiences

criteria.title: Style
criteria.description: Make sure radio is unique and stands out from other input options

criteria.title: Clickability
criteria.description: Consider what is clickable to make the radio option active (text label, container)

criteria.title: States
criteria.description: Radio can be default, active and disabled (see examples below)

resources.title: Style
resources.description: A container on a radio can improve it's clickability, but will take up more space. It's worth considering both options in your design system.

resources.title: States
resources.description: All the possible variations a radio can exist as depending on interaction and logic.

checklists.name: Searchbar
checklists.description: A search bar is an interactive input field that allows users to find specific content by entering keywords or phrases. It typically includes a text input area and a search icon/button, often enhanced with features like autocomplete suggestions to help users find information quickly.

criteria.title: Input field
criteria.description: A clear container for a user to start typing in

criteria.title: Label or placeholder text
criteria.description: Identify the purpose of the field is for them to search
criteria.suggestion: Use your placeholder text to suggest examples of what to search for

criteria.title: Quick links, autocomplete and suggestions
criteria.description: As the user is typing, offer available links and phrases based on what they have entered so far
criteria.suggestion: With enough data from the user, you can collect quick links and suggestions based on their previous searches to streamline their search

criteria.title: Submit search button
criteria.description: A visible link to submit search and view results
criteria.suggestion: Include a loading icon or feature once search has been submitted incase there is a connection issue

criteria.title: Previous searches
criteria.description: Showing what a user has searched before can speed up their experience if they frequently search the same queries

criteria.title: Appropriate visibility
criteria.description: Search should be directly linked to what you are looking for, whether it's searching across the entire platform or in a specific area

checklists.name: Tooltip
checklists.description: A tooltip is a small informational popup that appears when users hover over or focus on an element, providing additional context or explanations. It disappears when the user moves away, making it ideal for offering brief, helpful hints without cluttering the interface.

criteria.title: Information
criteria.description: Keep content clear and concise
criteria.suggestion: Information should be entirely relevant to what the tooltip is for, and elaborate on what is already visible

criteria.title: Contrast
criteria.description: The background should be different from the underlying content
criteria.suggestion: An inverse colour works best for contrast - if behind the tooltip is dominantly light, make the tooltip background dark with light text

criteria.title: Visibility
criteria.description: How a tooltip looks and shows
criteria.suggestion: A tooltip should activate on hover or select of an icon or text it is relevant to Only one tooltip should be visible at a time A tooltip should not cover the content it is relevant to

criteria.title: Dismiss action
criteria.description: Depending on how intrusive or extensive the tooltip is, a dismiss allows the user to feel more in control and allow the tooltip to feel more flexible and non-compulsory

resources.title: Interaction
resources.description: Tooltips typically appear through hover or focus, and disappear when leaving the trigger area, so it does not obstruct other information permanently.

resources.title: Additional description
resources.description: Tooltips may have another level of text if more context is needed, without making the title too overwhelming.

resources.title: Width
resources.description: Maintain readability with a limiting width, with a maximum value of 150-300px.

resources.title: Relative position
resources.description: Tooltips can dynamically appear relative to the interaction trigger, and its position can help reduce obstruction of other information.

resources.title: Use cases
resources.description: Tooltips can go beyond providing additional context. Consider their usage in revealing shortcuts, displaying statuses or previewing data.

checklists.name: Modal
checklists.description: A modal is a dialog box or popup window that appears on top of the main content, requiring user attention or interaction before returning to the main interface. It creates a focused experience by temporarily disabling the underlying page and dimming the background.

criteria.title: Title
criteria.description: Clear, simple text explaining the action of the modal
criteria.suggestion: Ensure your icon is recognisable in all possible sizes it's displayed at, and whether the detail needs to be simplified at a smaller size

criteria.title: Actionable item
criteria.description: A button or link to continue or close the event
criteria.suggestion: Users should always have an idea where they will be going to, or what event will happen before clicking a button If your button has generic copy such as 'Okay' or 'Cancel', include a label above it describing the event or purpose of the button

criteria.title: Close action
criteria.description: A way to exit the modal

criteria.title: Responsiveness
criteria.description: Consider the size of the modal on different device sizes, and whether a modal is suitable on all
criteria.suggestion: On mobile, adapt the modal to full screen to gain more space

criteria.title: Background change behind modal
criteria.description: Darken, blur or lighten - change the background behind the modal to bring focus to it

criteria.title: Description
criteria.description: Incase they require more information to understand how to make their decision

resources.title: Buttons
resources.description: Consider the button hierarchy and variations in a modal. It's common to have 2 contrasting button types that present opposing actions e.g. continue and cancel.

resources.title: Close action
resources.description: To dismiss the modal, but this can be a variable if you want to force the user to select a button to proceed, as the close action is a generic dismiss.

resources.title: Responsiveness
resources.description: A modal takes up a part of the desktop screen, but it is recommended to make a modal full size on mobile. This is incase the modal content requires scrolling, which is easier to interact with if the modal takes up the entire screen.

checklists.name: Loading
checklists.description: A loading indicator is a visual element that communicates to users that content or an action is being processed. It provides feedback through animations like spinning wheels, progress bars, or skeleton screens to maintain user engagement during wait times.

criteria.title: Visual indicator
criteria.description: A clear representation that content is loading or in progress of change

criteria.title: Text
criteria.description: Explaining the loading state
criteria.suggestion: Let the standard 'loading' text be a fallback, and try to be more specific e.g. 'adding your contacts, syncing your emails'

criteria.title: Time
criteria.description: Determine how long the time between two actions must be to require a loading component
criteria.suggestion: Don't interrupt two actions that instantly transition, but if there's a known 5 second period between two actions then the component is appropriate

criteria.title: Accessibility
criteria.description: Ensure your loading state can be clearly seen
criteria.suggestion: Place the loading indicator in a container to ensure accessibility, regardless of background If the loading indicator is on its own, create a version appropriate for light/dark backgrounds

criteria.title: Visuals
criteria.description: Entertain the user with an illustration during the loading state

resources.title: Style
resources.description: A loading indicator can have many different looks, the core principle must be that it shows a motion in loop or towards and endpoint.

resources.title: Text
resources.description: Text can help remind users what is happening and that they need to wait. It is optional, depending on how much space there is in the area that is loading.

resources.title: Context (optional)
resources.description: It doesn't just have to be 'loading'. The loading text can be specific to what action is being run. There's also a chance here to add some personality, as waiting for something to load is typically a mundane experience.

checklists.name: Toggle
checklists.description: A toggle is a switch-like control that allows users to quickly alternate between two opposing states (on/off) with a single click or tap.

criteria.title: Context
criteria.description: Explaining what the toggle will do
criteria.suggestion: A toggle should always be turning a function on or off, not between two opposing versions of a function e.g. hot or cold Consider toggles for straightforward decisions that have low risk implications

criteria.title: Transition
criteria.description: A clear visual change of the toggle switching between different states

criteria.title: State
criteria.description: How the button changes based on the interaction, examples below
criteria.suggestion: Contrast active and inactive with brand colour for active and keeping the inactive muted

resources.title: Default
resources.description: Toggles are usually off by default. It allows users to explicitly opt in to the action, rather than being opted in automatically deceptively.

resources.title: Active
resources.description: Toggle is on meaning it is actively performing an action. The active state can utilise the brand colours to help it feel part of the UI.

resources.title: With label
resources.description: The label should convey the action or state of the toggle being active. For example, the label stating 'silent mode' means if the toggle is active, silent mode is active.

checklists.name: Input Field
checklists.description: An input field is an interactive area where users can enter and edit text or data. It provides a clear visual container for user input, often accompanied by labels and validation feedback, making it essential for forms and data collection interfaces.

criteria.title: Input field
criteria.description: Interactive text field for user to enter their data into
criteria.suggestion: Ensure text size is readable on all devices

criteria.title: Label
criteria.description: Stating what information the user is meant to provide
criteria.suggestion: Avoid all caps for text labels to improve readability

criteria.title: Placeholder text
criteria.description: Text inside the input field acting as an example of what you want the user to enter
criteria.suggestion: Text colour must be notably lighter than default text, so users don't assume its filled in Providing examples lets users understand how you would like them to enter the information

criteria.title: Data format
criteria.description: Set text fields to allow the relevant text values e.g. numeric only for phone number
criteria.suggestion: Hint at preferred data format with placeholder text or hint

criteria.title: Illustration or icon
criteria.description: A visual cue can help break up a long list of text fields

criteria.title: Hint
criteria.description: Elaborate on the title of the text field incase a user struggles to know what to enter

resources.title: Style
resources.description: Style of the field container establishes visual hierarchy and accessibility, and should be consistent with branding.

resources.title: Labels and hints
resources.description: Both are essential context and guidance. Labels are required as they succintly call out what information is needed, while hints elaborate on context, instructions or formatting.

resources.title: Icons
resources.description: There are two types of icons for input fields: leading and trailing. A leading icon is typically for visually representing the context of the field, helping differentiate it from others. A trailing icon is typically an action that can trigger behaviour in the field.

resources.title: States
resources.description: A breakdown of all different interactions with an input field

resources.title: Sizes
resources.description: An optional flexibility in the case of navigating spacing constraints and/or creating a balanced interface based on surrounding elements

resources.title: Area
resources.description: While input fields are the common default, input areas allow for larger content to be entered and viewed. They can also provide an expectation of how much to write

checklists.name: Icon
checklists.description: An icon is a small, symbolic visual element that represents an action, feature, or concept. It's purpose is to communicate meaning quickly, save space, and enhance visual navigation across an interface.

criteria.title: Responsiveness
criteria.description: The flexibility in detail of the icons at varying sizes
criteria.suggestion: Ensure your icon is recognisable in all possible sizes it's displayed at, and whether the detail needs to be simplified at a smaller size

criteria.title: Visual style consistency
criteria.description: All icons share the same stroke weight, corner radius, and optical sizing approach

criteria.title: Color
criteria.description: Black and white, flat colors or gradients
criteria.suggestion: Incorporate your branding colours into the style

criteria.title: Naming
criteria.description: Name an icon by what it literally is so it can be used flexibly
criteria.suggestion: Don't name an icon based on an action so it stays adaptable e.g. a pencil icon shouldn't be named "edit", as it could be used for another purpose elsewhere

resources.title: Styles
resources.description: Fill, outline, sharp or rounded — what matters most is that it's consistent!

resources.title: Sizes
resources.description: Systemising the icon sizes makes it easier to implement

resources.title: Naming
resources.description: Icon names can be based on an action but should also include the literal meaning too e.g. a pencil icon is commonly used for edit, but should still include the name 'pencil'

criteria.title: Table header
criteria.description: The value of each column to provide structure for the row content
criteria.suggestion: Fix your header on scroll to continue giving context to user

criteria.title: Row style
criteria.description: Borders and contrasting background colours can be explored to differentiate

criteria.title: Spacing
criteria.description: Define the consistent padding of each row and the header

criteria.title: Search
criteria.description: The ability to find a specific keyword or row
criteria.suggestion: Ensure all of your possible data points can be searched and defined by text input

criteria.title: Actions
criteria.description: Performing a task based on the row and information seen e.g. view, edit, delete

criteria.title: Filter and sort
criteria.description: Allow users to customise what they want to see in the table and in which order

criteria.title: Responsiveness
criteria.description: Determine the structure on significantly smaller devices - whether the information collapses into an accordion for example
criteria.suggestion: Horizontal scrolling is an alternative to rethinking a new layout

criteria.title: Pagination
criteria.description: Breakpoints in the table for digesting information in parts

checklists.name: Card
checklists.description: A card is a contained, modular component that groups related information and actions. It displays content like text, images, and interactive elements within a distinct container, often with shadows or borders to create visual hierarchy and organization in layouts.

criteria.title: Style
criteria.description: Consider default background, border, shadow

criteria.title: Consistency
criteria.description: Ensure you have one base style for all cards

criteria.title: Spacing
criteria.description: A framework to sort your padding levels by
criteria.suggestion: Choose an easily divisible number as your padding difference, like divided by 4 or 5

criteria.title: Responsiveness
criteria.description: Consider the structure of the content in all various screen sizes
criteria.suggestion: Adopt a 'top-down' approach on mobile to not overfill the rows

criteria.title: Content hierarchy
criteria.description: The primary action/s you want users to perform
criteria.suggestion: Display links at the end of the card so the user is informed by the content in the card before making a decision

resources.title: Style
resources.description: Card style should be consistent across the product, with levels of a particular style e.g. different levels of shadows on all cards.

resources.title: Spacing
resources.description: This can be a series of numeric values. The most common is multiples of 4 (8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, etc).

resources.title: Radius
resources.description: Border radius of cards should be consistent across the product

checklists.name: Button
checklists.description: A button is an interactive element that triggers an action when clicked or tapped. It clearly communicates its clickability through visual styling and provides feedback on user interaction, making it a fundamental component for enabling user actions in interfaces.

criteria.title: Base style
criteria.description: Your default style, one of the following: fill, outline, underline

criteria.title: Shape
criteria.description: Visual properties of a button: padding, border, border radius, shadow

criteria.title: Variants
criteria.description: Each visual type to represent button structure e.g. primary and secondary buttons

criteria.title: Copy
criteria.description: Instructional text that details what will happen if you click the button
criteria.suggestion: Users should understand what will happen before clicking a button. Buttons can have generic copy such as 'Okay' or 'Cancel', but only if there is context around that action, in the title or as a label for example.

criteria.title: States
criteria.description: How the button changes based on the interaction: hover, focused, disabled

resources.title: Sizes
resources.description: Having multiple sizes helps with a complex interface that has several actions.

resources.title: States
resources.description: To help indicate an interaction (or lack of one) on a button. These are the 4 standard but there are many more.

resources.title: Icons
resources.description: Icons can help differentiate buttons, and familiarise a user with an action using a visual they recognise

resources.title: Style
resources.description: Style can help establish hierarchy. The number of styles should depend on the experience

checklists.name: Badge
checklists.description: A badge is a small visual indicator that displays short, dynamic information like counts or status. It typically appears as a colored circle or pill shape, often overlaid on other elements.

criteria.title: Detail
criteria.description: A badge can have a numeric value, or a basic shape
criteria.suggestion: A basic shape like a small circle is effective in conveying one update, while numeric value represents the amount of updates

criteria.title: Color
criteria.description: Badges can represent your standard states - error, success, warning
criteria.suggestion: Be consistent in the details - outlines, shadows, perspective, corners and colours

criteria.title: Offset position
criteria.description: A badge should sit outside it's relevant element to gain attention easier

resources.title: Number count
resources.description: A badge number can indicate an amount of unread items like messages or notifications

resources.title: Dot
resources.description: Just a dot is a more subtle option to indicate there is unread items, without including how many

checklists.name: Avatar
checklists.description: An avatar is a visual representation of a user. It helps identify individuals across a digital interface, commonly used in user profiles, comment sections, and chat applications.

criteria.title: Visualiser
criteria.description: Show what the avatar looks like before posting or updating

criteria.title: Link to upload or select avatar
criteria.description: Accessible link for a user to select
criteria.suggestion: If you want the avatar visual itself to be clickable to change, add an indicator on it to show it's editable from that source e.g. a pencil icon

criteria.title: Placeholder image
criteria.description: If a user hasn't uploaded or added an avatar yet there should be a placeholder e.g. a default icon, or the user's initials

criteria.title: Acceptable file types
criteria.description: Tell the user what file types are allowed (JPEG, PNG, SVG)

criteria.title: Status change updating avatar
criteria.description: This doesn't have to be apart of the avatar component (it can be a banner or toast for example), but it is possible to incorporate it

criteria.title: Alternatives
criteria.description: If a user doesn't want to upload an image, offer an illustrative alternative, as it's better than nothing and can still convey their personality

criteria.title: Editing uploaded avatar
criteria.description: Allow a user to crop and resize their avatar before saving it

resources.title: Shape
resources.description: An avatar can be rounded in several ways, but what matters most is establishing a consistent shape.

resources.title: Size
resources.description: Having pre-determined sizes can help apply an avatar across multiple scenarios.

resources.title: Status
resources.description: Accompanying an avatar can be a symbol indicating status, verification and more.

resources.title: Fallback
resources.description: Incase a user doesn't want to upload an avatar, it's important to have fallbacks so the component can still appear in the UI.

checklists.name: Dropdown Menu
checklists.description: A dropdown triggered from a button or right-click target to reveal a menu of actions the user can proceed with

criteria.title: Trigger affordance
criteria.description: The element that opens the menu: an overflow icon, chevron button, or right-click target

criteria.title: Menu item anatomy
criteria.description: The structure of each action: label, optional leading icon, optional trailing shortcut, optional destructive styling
criteria.suggestion: Mixing icon and non-icon items in the same list throws off the scan

criteria.title: Section dividers and groups
criteria.description: Dividers and/or labels that break related actions into sections once the menu gets large

criteria.title: Destructive item styling
criteria.description: Visual differentiation — typically the danger colour — for actions that cannot be undone
criteria.suggestion: Always place destructive actions at the end of the menu, after a divider to reduce misclicks

criteria.title: Nested submenu
criteria.description: A secondary menu triggered by a parent item, used for grouping related but distinct actions
criteria.suggestion: Limit nesting to one level to be too layered and confusing

criteria.title: Disabled items
criteria.description: Menu items that are visible but cannot be triggered, indicating an unavailable action
criteria.suggestion: A tooltip on that item that reveals the reason it is disabled is handy

criteria.title: Positioning and overflow
criteria.description: The menu's placement relative to its trigger, repositioning automatically to stay within the viewport

criteria.title: Keyboard shortcut display
criteria.description: Shortcut hints aligned to the trailing edge of the item label

checklists.name: Adding to cart
checklists.description: Shopping online means users need to easily add products they want to their cart. This fundamental action can make or break a sale, so getting it right is crucial.

resources.title: Outline variant selection for product
resources.description: Whether it’s size, colour, amount or something else, it must be clear what details must be picked to be able to add an item to cart.

resources.title: Primary action on product page is add to cart
resources.description: One of if not the most prominent button on the page to draw the user’s attention. This may change if you want an 'add to cart' button on a grid view of multiple products.

resources.title: Feedback once added
resources.description: Immediate confirmation the item has been added. This can be done several ways and depends on the amount of intrusion you want to have, which is why 2 options are shown.

resources.title: Link to cart view
resources.description: Typically in a primary navigation, so that if the user continues shopping but is then ready to checkout, the cart is easily accessible. Showing the number of products is a way to catch their attention that they have items added but not purchased yet. A total price can also be considered to be shown.

resources.title: Empty state
resources.description: Show a clear visual placeholder with an upload icon and simple text that indicate a file can be dropped into the area to upload. It’s also suitable to offer a click to upload route incase a user prefers that option.

resources.title: Drag and drop interaction
resources.description: When a file is across the interaction canvas, there should be a clear visual state change to indicate it has detected a file attempting to be dropped. This lets the user know it’s safe to release the file at this point.

resources.title: Progress indicator
resources.description: Display progress that updates in real-time so users know their upload is working. If a percentage is not possible to show, a loading indicator can at least show that something is happening. Include file names and show overall progress when uploading multiple files to keep users informed throughout the process.

resources.title: File restrictions & constraints
resources.description: Clearly state limits to what files can be uploaded. This is commonly file size and format, shown in the upload area before users attempt to upload files. If a user tries to upload a file outside the constraints, an error message should show explaining it does follow the constraints.

resources.title: Outcome status
resources.description: Use visual indicators like green checkmarks for successful uploads and red warning icons for failures. For failures, include an error message explaining what went wrong and what users can do to fix it.

resources.title: Upload actions
resources.description: Ways to interact with an upload. Choose which actions to show by default vs on hover based on available space, aiming to avoid overwhelming users with too many visible options. Common actions include: Retry failed uploads Cancel upload in progress Delete files Rename files

resources.title: Showing multiple uploaded files
resources.description: Display files in a clean list or grid with thumbnails when possible, and ensure the layout you choose is scalable. What information you show about each file depends on the context of the upload. A file name or size can be relevant in one case, while seeing the images uploaded can be the relevant detail in another.

checklists.name: Verifying account
checklists.description: Verification is a critical role to promise security for a user in the early phases of onboarding, which means it must be a smooth experience that feels helps rather than burdensome.

resources.title: Establish a trigger point
resources.description: Clearly indicate when verification is required, giving context as to why verification is necessary. It is common to verify the email or phone number used for account creation, because this is ensuring the person with access to those details is the same person creating the account.

resources.title: Method selection (optional)
resources.description: Depending on the level of sophistication you want to offer, you can make multiple verification methods available (email, SMS, authenticator). The common default is what the user is using to sign up with e.g. if signing up with email address, send code to email.

resources.title: Confirm delivery and contact information used
resources.description: Display the email address or phone number where the verification will be sent so the user can see it is the correct destination. That way if they have not received a code and the contact information provided was incorrect, they can see this, go back, and enter the correct value.

resources.title: Ability to input verification code
resources.description: The input field can be intuitive to show a field per digit, but the default input field is perfectly accessible.

resources.title: Incorrect value (and resend option)
resources.description: Provide specific error messages for different failure scenarios and clear next steps: Expired code: offer link to send a new code Incorrect code: ask to check email/SMS again or offer link to send new code Too many incorrect attempts: contact support team or wait for defined time period before trying again

resources.title: Verification success state
resources.description: Display clear confirmation when verification succeeds and continue to next step of interface.

checklists.name: Canceling subscription
checklists.description: Similar to closing an account, a user can decide to end their experience and stop paying for your product. Just because they're leaving doesn't mean we can't give them a graceful exit. It's important to make a cancelation obvious to find and easy to travel through.

resources.title: Show a link in account details
resources.description: This doesn't have to be the first or most prominent link, but it should be clearly visible. If you're unsure about including it on the account page, it's suitable to place on the billing settings.

resources.title: Confirm intent to cancel
resources.description: Sometimes, a user misclicks. So it's okay to ask if they're sure they want to make this choice, and not just automatically canceling their subscription. But... while the user is there, you can attempt a last ditch effort to reel them back (it cannot be pressuring or manipulative). If the product can only be access with a subscription, you can remind them of the product's value. If the product can be access in a free version, you can remind them of that specific subscription's value.

resources.title: Request a reason for canceling (optional)
resources.description: It can be helpful to receive feedback on why a user is canceling. Too expensive? Competitor preferred? Just don't need it anymore? It's an easy way to start identifying the key factors affecting churn.

resources.title: Confirm subscription has been canceled
resources.description: Now that it's canceled, make sure you tell the user when their subscription is active until.

checklists.name: Filtering items
checklists.description: Filtering helps users find what they need in large collections by specifying specific values of properties the items contain.

resources.title: Show action near item collection
resources.description: Place above or beside the collection it affects, using a recognizable icons and/or label.

resources.title: Show available filter options
resources.description: When the action is triggered, filter options can either be shown on the same page for immediate feedback, or on another page. This should be dependent on the amount of filtering that is possible, and whether you think the user is likelier to tweak filters ongoing, or apply several and then view results. It's also worthwhile considering a filtering priority order, with the most common options filtered sitting at the front.

resources.title: Consider different filter types
resources.description: The standard filter is a multi-select option picker. But certain properties can benefit from a different way of managing the filtering. There's sliders, checkboxes, dropdowns and others to consider. Each property should be considered, asking yourself what feels like the easiest way to change this value.

resources.title: Show active filters clearly when applied
resources.description: On the item collection page, display which filters are currently applied. You can also choose to have a high level active state applied to the filter action to imply it is in use, if you find showing all applied filters is too cluttered.

resources.title: Provide easy filter removal
resources.description: Let users clear individual filters or all filters at once to allow easier refining of their results.

resources.title: Show result count
resources.description: Not a must have, but this can be handy where it is meaningful for users to see what the total results value has reduced to. It will help users feel if their result is too narrow or broad, directing them to either add or remove filters.

resources.title: Empty state
resources.description: It's possible that a combination of filters can product no results. Explain this clearly and suggest adjusting or clearing filters to see results.

checklists.name: Saving changes
checklists.description: Users are constantly updating their details. They might be changing an email address, fixing a typo in their name, or updating their payment details. That's why it's important to confirm that a change has been saved, in the clearest way. Here's a breakdown of how changes being saved should look and feel like.

resources.title: Show action that enables change
resources.description: There should be an action to enable information to be updated. It may be automatically editable, but that can be riskier for some software. If it is read-only by default, then a button can trigger the editable version to then update and save.

resources.title: Disable save action until changes are made
resources.description: An action should be visible as a source of confirming changes to be saved - this is usually a button. Initially, the action can be disabled. It indicates no changes have been made, and there is nothing to save. A common location for this action is in the navigation above the fold, so it's always visible over the content. Another option is after all the content that's editable.

resources.title: State changes to active once a change is made
resources.description: In the example, we've changed the email address, which means a change is waiting to be saved. Changing the button state to active brings the user's attention to the action.

resources.title: Action changes to loading state when pressed
resources.description: Now that the changes are being saved, you want to show that action is in progress. You can do so with a loading spinner in the action, as the user's view will be on that element.

resources.title: Notify changes have been saved
resources.description: The page will reload or update, and this is the critical part. The user should now be informed that their changes have been saved. They can now safely leave the page, knowing the details are locked in until they choose to change them again.

checklists.name: Entering promo code
checklists.description: A reward for a user to earn a discount on their purchase, promo codes are a pre-requisite in any e-commerce website. ‍ To avoid a confused customer, make sure they understand what is happening with their code - whether it works, expired or isn't applicable.

resources.title: Show promo code input field
resources.description: The cart or checkout are pages expected to have a promo code field. It should be in a place that can be seen when scanning towards the button to continue.

resources.title: Promo code applied successfully
resources.description: The change can be reflected using your success state colors (likely green) to indicate the code was applied. In the example is two different options, divided by how much information you want to show. For both, hiding the input field altogether makes it clear only one code can be entered.

resources.title: Reflect promo code impact
resources.description: This can be shown with the promo code entry as a total amount, or be represented on In item-to-item basis. It's important to also show or at least repeat the discount near the total at checkout.

resources.title: Promo code error
resources.description: The promo code may not be applicable, or entered incorrectly.

resources.title: Remove promo code
resources.description: In some cases, a user might not like the discount offered and prefer the original sale price of an item. Or, they found a better promo code to use.

checklists.name: Showing input error
checklists.description: Users mistype all the time - whether it's a finger slipping or rushing through letters, errors happen. So for an everyday occurrence, solving an error should be obvious and seamless. The key parts of making that happen are strong visuals, clear communication, and state changes — which are all featured below.

resources.title: Keep the input in default state
resources.description: The text field should be checked for errors only after the information has been entered.

resources.title: Allow user to enter information
resources.description: Let the user type without interruptions and submit the information aka don't assess as changes are made.

resources.title: Signal error after loss of focus
resources.description: After the input has lost focus (user has clicked another element), the field should be assessed. Looks like we have an error here! In this case, explain why the error happened, and what is required to resolve it. For accessibility, combine the text with a visual icon that indicates an error was found.

resources.title: Return to default state upon reattempt
resources.description: Once the user focuses on the field again, the error message should disappear. If there is an error again, the process will simply repeat until they are able to continue.

checklists.name: Resetting password
checklists.description: Every now and then, a user can't remember their password to log back in. Luckily, it's a straightforward process to change it. It's important to make the experience feel straightforward, so the user feels like they've gotten back into their account as smooth as possible.

resources.title: Place reset link close to password field
resources.description: Style it as a link to show it is clickable

resources.title: Ask for account details to verify
resources.description: In this case it's usually the email address that's requested, because it can recognise your account and be the channel the link is securely sent to. Note: If the user already entered their email address on the previous login page, that can be prefill this field and speed up the flow!

resources.title: Show information has been sent
resources.description: Based on the account information provided in Step 2, explain how they can continue. If an email was provided, send an email for the next step. If a mobile number was provided, send a code or link to open.

resources.title: The message sent explains next steps
resources.description: This could be a link to a page that allows the user to reset their password. It could also be a code for the user to provide on a page to verify their account, to then reset their password.

resources.title: Reset the password!
resources.description: Whether it's a verification code or a link to click behind an email address, the next page should be a clear text field to enter a new password. You can provide guidelines if you have requirements for the password to pass a threshold of strength to be accepted.

resources.title: Password successfully reset
resources.description: After the password has been reset, indicate the successful and push their momentum to their initial intent: logging in.

checklists.name: Deleting account
checklists.description: Sometimes it's just not meant to be, and that's okay. Users come and go, so it's important to recognise your solution is only for some and not for all. For those who want to leave, make it as simple as possible. You can try to understand why they're leaving, but don't get too in the way. ‍ There's no need to be passive aggressive or guilt tripping. They'll remember it, and likely share the experience with others who will reconsider your product.

resources.title: Show a link to delete account
resources.description: Don't make this difficult. This link should be visible in the profile or settings of a product. It should also be available in the support area.

resources.title: Politely ask for feedback
resources.description: It helps to know why somebody is choosing to leave. But, it should not be pressured or forcefully asked. Convey the request feedback to improve other people's experience and to also consider their personal reasons.

resources.title: Explain what it means to delete the account before confirming
resources.description: Be clear with what happens to the account and the information in it should a user close. Is all the data permanently deleted? Can they come back and restore their account? Is the deletion immediate, or can they use their account until a certain date?

resources.title: Confirm account has been deleted
resources.description: Now that their account is deleted and it's finally complete, embrace that! Be comfortable acknowledging they have left. Do not show any passive aggressiveness.

checklists.name: Contacting support
checklists.description: If there's ever a problem, a user should know how to get help. Then when they try to get that help, they should know exactly what kind of communication they're receiving. Making support not only available but suitable to how users tackle a problem is important on being on the right track together. If you're explaining to a user in text where the interface elements are when a screenshot would tell a much clearer story, then that's the first problem to solve before you even get to theirs.

resources.title: Show a link to contact support
resources.description: This can be placed in a number of areas, such as: ‍ • footer in a website • settings in a mobile app • a page experiencing an error Use clear copy and easy to recognise visuals to highlight the link.

resources.title: Show methods of contact
resources.description: If you have one option, showcase it! If you have multiple options (chat, call, FAQ), list them out and represent each of their benefits. Chat is great for a specific, complicated issue that needs an instant response. On the other hand, FAQ is great for standard questions that are easy to explain. Also consider the order of the methods. A FAQ as the first option is great because it lets a user find their own answer without waiting on you to respond. But a direct chat can be seen as more convenient as it's less direct troubleshooting for the user.

resources.title: Outline how to communicate and what is expected
resources.description: Once a method is chosen, make it clear on how the method will work. Illustrate the response time, and what the user will need to provide to receive support.

checklists.name: Making a card payment
checklists.description: When paying for something online, two thoughts will come to mind for the user: is this safe, and is this clear? A well-designed payment experience covers these by communicating what's happening with a user's money, and that it's all happening securely. Below are the steps a user will take to submit a card payment, and what factors you'll need to consider.

resources.title: Offer payment methods
resources.description: Other methods can be shown, but for this flow we'll focus on the user selecting 'credit or debit card'. This is because it's the one with the most internal effort on designing and building, compared to other services which are often third-party integrations.

resources.title: Request card details
resources.description: Show all relevant text fields to complete. Consider the size of these fields relative to the details entered. Note: in a product where the user is revisiting and saved payment methods are available, consider a flow that allows the user to add/remove payment methods.

resources.title: Submit payment with card details entered
resources.description: It's also important to consider validation before a user submits their details. Numbers can be mistyped, the card may have expired - so make sure these numerous error states are addressed.

resources.title: Show payment processing
resources.description: A payment may not be triggered instantly, taking a few seconds (or minutes). A loading page is crucial to calm the user’s nerves in regards to what’s happening to their money.

resources.title: Confirmation payment processed successfully
resources.description: It’s a success! Clearly indicate to the user that their payment was processed, and the funds was received.

resources.title: Outline next steps
resources.description: What now? Does the payment trigger something? If so, let the user know. Example 1: a physical product has been purchased. Once the payment has processed, tell the user the order is in motion. Example 2: a user signed up for a subscription. Offer a link to continue to the product to start using it.

checklists.name: Submitting a form
checklists.description: A form can help a user achieve anything from creating an account to subscribing to a newsletter. They are often the last step of a user's journey, so should be quick and easy to complete.

resources.title: Show button to submit
resources.description: Below the form fields, a button to submit the information needs to be present. You can change the copy to fit the form e.g. the button can say “Subscribe” if someone is providing their email address to receive emails.

resources.title: Show loading state after submission
resources.description: The user must see the form is in the process of being submitted. Note: also make sure your hover state is considered before they press the button!

resources.title: Show success message when it submits
resources.description: The form was submitted! Let’s communicate that back to the user with a clear success message.

resources.title: If it doesn't, show an error message
resources.description: Sometimes, things don’t work out. If the form can’t submit, because of invalid information or another error, that also needs to be shown.

resources.title: An error may occur because of the wrong information
resources.description: If the criteria for a text field isn’t met, the form can fail to submit due to that error, and must be detailed.

checklists.name: Action Sheet
checklists.description: The sheet that slides up from the bottom of the screen to present options or confirmations — the mobile equivalent of a dropdown menu or modal dialog.

criteria.title: Heading and actions
criteria.description: Similar to modals, there must be a clear heading outline the purpose of the action sheet, along with relevant actions the user can select to continue

criteria.title: Swipe or backdrop dismiss
criteria.description: The sheet is dismissible by dragging it down or tapping the dimmed area behind it, along with the expected close button

criteria.title: Destructive action styling
criteria.description: Any destructive option — delete, remove, block — styled in red and positioned last, separated from safe actions.
criteria.suggestion: Users scan top-to-bottom and tap quickly — a destructive action buried at the bottom prevents accidental taps.

criteria.title: Cancel action
criteria.description: A clearly labelled cancel/close option that dismisses the sheet without taking any action
criteria.suggestion: Typically the secondary action, similar to a desktop modal

criteria.title: Snap points (if expandable)
criteria.description: Defining where the action sheet expands or compresses to on resize, instead of it being free-form
criteria.suggestion: A drag handle at the top of the sheet indicates the action sheet can be expanded (or dismissed)

criteria.title: Content scrollability
criteria.description: Consider what stickies as you scroll so the sheet remains contextual, and that the sheet stays fixed in position on scroll
criteria.suggestion: Similar to modals, it's best to avoid scrollability here unless you cannot avoid it

criteria.title: Keyboard relation
criteria.description: Consider the action sheet size and responsiveness if keyboard needs to be triggered while it is active

criteria.title: Backdrop dimming
criteria.description: The screen behind darkened to draw focus to the action sheet

checklists.name: Billing
checklists.description: Payment history, receipts, and everything related to how the user is charged.

criteria.title: Manage via App Store
criteria.description: A link or prompt directing users to the App Store or Play Store to manage their subscription
criteria.suggestion: Apple and Google require subscription management to happen through their platform, so a buried path there is a consistent source of support contacts and poor reviews

criteria.title: Next billing date and amount
criteria.description: The next scheduled payment date and amount visible without needing to dig into billing history
criteria.suggestion: Surfacing this proactively reduces cancellations driven by surprise charges

criteria.title: Billing history and receipts
criteria.description: A list of past charges with amounts and dates, with individual receipts accessible
criteria.suggestion: Particularly important for users paying with a work card, who often need receipts for expense reporting

criteria.title: Restore purchases
criteria.description: A button to restore previously purchased subscriptions or in-app purchases after reinstalling or signing in on a new device
criteria.suggestion: Required by Apple for apps with in-app purchases, since it solves the common case of reinstalling after a device change

criteria.title: Refund help link
criteria.description: Guidance on how to request a refund, typically via the platform's own process
criteria.suggestion: Refunds are handled by Apple or Google, not the app directly, and making this clear reduces confusion and support volume

criteria.title: Tax display
criteria.description: Tax or VAT amounts displayed separately from the base price where legally required.

checklists.name: Camera
checklists.description: Capturing photos, video, or documents as well as reviewing and customising the capture experience for accessing the phone camera within an app.

criteria.title: Permission request
criteria.description: Camera permission requested at the moment capture is triggered (not on app launch or during onboarding)
